This study examines gravitational wave (GW) signatures originating from primordial electromagnetic (EM) fields, specifically targeting signal characteristics within the Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) band. We analyze two distinct scenarios: an EM field existing in the early universe and one generated in the early solar system. In the cosmological scenario, the EM field exerts extra pressure, altering the evolution of primordial density fluctuations and producing unique GW spectra. Conversely, an early solar system EM field acts as a GW source through its quadrupole moment, with both cases showing a dependence on the initial EM field amplitude. Additionally, an EM field arising in the early solar system could explain recent anomalies observed in the PTA data, whereas an origin in the cosmological era would manifest primarily as a GW stochastic background.

We introduce a new approach for compressing light field data that uniquely integrates spatial information to guide both encoding and decoding processes. By employing a disparity-aware model, our method ensures consistent handling of varying image disparities throughout the reconstruction pipeline. This strategy is designed to enhance overall visual quality, particularly in areas that are difficult to compress. To achieve this, we utilize a novel V2V (View-to-View) prediction technique grounded in optical flow, which constructs a motion-aware intermediate layer specifically for encoding both high-disparity and low-disparity regions. This approach is further bolstered by a novel V3V (View-to-View) prediction mechanism utilizing a 3D convolutional network to refine the encoding stage. During decoding, a 3D convolutional network is employed to generate a disparity-aware representation from the encoded high-resolution view, which is then leveraged to sustain high compression performance. Experimental results demonstrate that, across four publicly available light field datasets, the proposed framework delivers state-of-the-art compression ratios exceeding 10:1 while maintaining PSNR levels above 30 dB.

This study investigates a new hybrid approach combining the interactive (IRWIN) and non-interactive (NMWIN) window mechanisms to enhance vectorized cross-lingual information retrieval (i.e., vector-based XLI). While a standard NMWIN method is designed to be robust and efficient, it often overlooks the relevance of words located outside the selected window. Conversely, an IRWIN method dynamically adjusts the window size based on the specific context of each query, though it may still be constrained by fixed window dimensions. We introduce a hybrid strategy that leverages the reliability and speed of NMWIN alongside the adaptive capabilities provided by IRWIN. By integrating these frameworks, our proposed model is capable of learning optimal parameters for pre-defined windows and applying this to various vectorized XLI models. Empirical evaluations on the XLIQ and XLIQD benchmarks demonstrate that our hybrid method significantly outperforms both standalone IRWIN and standard non-interactive approaches.

This paper evaluates the performance of various small-area estimation (SAE) techniques applied to a survey of 11,000 households across Ghana, specifically targeting household food security status. The analysis focuses on estimating food security prevalence within small geographic areas defined by district and municipality, with a minimum of approximately 100 households per group. Due to the limited number of observations per small area and the high dimensionality of the resulting linear mixed models, standard estimation methods for linear and nonlinear random effects models proved inadequate. To address this, I developed a robust nonlinear-in-means SAE capable of handling nonlinear submodel specifications, alongside a new approximation technique for linear SAEs that yields numerically stable and precise parameter estimates. The proposed methods were benchmarked against benchmark results from established linear and nonlinear estimation techniques. The findings indicate that a nonlinear-in-means SAE with a linear-submodel approximation offers a viable solution for high-dimensional linear SAE problems, producing estimates nearly identical to those derived from full maximum likelihood estimation. Furthermore, numerical simulations reveal that both linear and nonlinear SAE estimators are reliable for small-area inference. The study concludes by outlining the implementation steps and computational advantages of these new methods.

This study presents a theoretical analysis of the rare decay process $\Sigma^+ \to p\mu^+ \mu^-$, utilizing the Lagrangian effective field theory (L.EFT) framework. Within this model, the proton serves as the sole hadronic participant, allowing for a tractable theoretical description. We demonstrate that the decay amplitude can be explicitly decomposed into contributions from the electromagnetic and weak sectors. The findings indicate that the electromagnetic force dominates the process, whereas the weak sector's influence remains negligible. Additionally, we explore the implications of CPT violation in the $\Sigma^+ \to \Lambda^+ \to p\mu^+ \mu^-$. We establish that the decay rate for the $\Sigma^+ \to p\mu^+ \mu^- \mu^-$ process is approximately $10^{-13}$ times more sensitive than the standard neutron-to-proton decay ratio ($n \to p e^+ \mu^-$) in terms of CPT violation parameters. This heightened sensitivity suggests that the experimental sensitivity to CPT violation parameters in the $\Sigma^+ \to p\mu^+ \mu^- \mu^-$ decay could potentially surpass that achieved through standard neutron decay experiments.

The formation of planets occurs within disks surrounding young stars, specifically within protoplanetary disks. While it is hypothesized that these disks originate from disks found in their parent molecular clouds (pre-stellar cores), the specific mechanism linking a collapsing core-disk system to a formed disk has not been adequately explored. In this work, we examine protostellar disk formation by employing high-resolution 3D magnetohydrodynamic simulations that track the evolution of a young star system from its parent pre-stellar core stage. We demonstrate that angular momentum conservation drives disk creation: as a protostar forms from a collapsing cloud, a significant fraction of infalling matter possesses high specific angular momentum, which cannot accrete onto the young star and instead establishes the disk. We calculated the properties of these disks using a standard MMSN core model for their parent clouds, finding that a significant portion of the resulting disks are thinner than the mottened one, suggesting a more complex formation process. This work addresses the series completion problem, which involves predicting missing data points in temporal sequences. Although existing deep learning methods achieve strong performance, they often fail to capture temporal patterns effectively and lack the ability to identify the most critical time periods for prediction. To overcome these limitations, we present a novel deep temporal series model featuring learnable time gates integrated with a Bayesian framework enhanced by the variational elbow prior. The purpose of these time gates is to selectively emphasize specific periods deemed most informative for forecasting, while the elbow prior enforces sparsity in the gate activation weights, thereby further isolating the most significant times. We employ the variational elbow prior within a maximum posterior estimation procedure to approximate the series distribution. For computational efficiency, we derive an analytical closed-form solution for the variational posterior over the latent continuous states, eliminating the need for Monte Carlo sampling. Furthermore, we introduce a variational elbow state-space layer compatible with traditional State-space Deep Learning architectures. Empirical evaluations on multiple public datasets demonstrate that our proposed general deep temporal series model substantially boosts predictive accuracy.

This paper critiques the paper "Steeds-Truths: An alternative to classical two-valued logic" by Bagnara et al., which employs non-two-valued steady algorithms to represent sets of possible execution paths for software systems. In doing so, Bagnara et al. utilize Pontryagin duality and strengthenings of the negation operator within classical two-valued semantics to define their "steadfast negation." Our critique demonstrates that utilizing duality in this context is unnecessary and that the observed correspondence between the sets of possible paths and the dual group of integers arises naturally from an equivalence between their respective generating groups—namely, the two-cyclic group and the infinite-cyclic group—rather than requiring dualities. Specifically, this relationship is a manifestation of the isomorphism \( \mathbb{Z}_2 \cong \mathbb{Z} \), resolved via Homomorphism Theorem principles. Consequently, this framework allows for a straightforward approach to understanding "steadfast negation" without recourse to duality, utilizing principles of universal algebra and group homomorphism. In doing so, this method also elucidates why this steadfast negation is functionally identical to the "Kleene's negation" used in three-valued logic, thereby clarifying the underlying mathematical structure shared between these models.

This study introduces a technique to mitigate bias and enhance fairness within Federated Learning (FL) while simultaneously ensuring privacy in the presence of adversaries. Unlike centralized deep learning models, FL operates by processing data across multiple devices, where the server periodically requests updated model parameters from participants. Participants then transmit these updates, often perturbed using differential privacy techniques, back to the server for aggregation. The aggregated results form the foundation for the next training cycle. Despite the privacy safeguards in FL, issues such as equity bias and adversarial risks persist. This research demonstrates the efficacy of our proposed Fair Federated Learning (FED-EP) framework, which leverages trimmed mean aggregation to foster fairness, and further strengthens privacy by applying a privacy budget. Our experimental evaluations on diverse datasets—including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and FashionMNIST—along with various client configurations, substantiate the efficacy of FED-EP.

We present a $U(1)_X$ extension of the Standard Model (SM) that incorporates three right-handed (RH) Majorana neutrinos and an $SU(2)_L$-charged scalar doublet. This model is embedded within a supersymmetric minimum framework, where the SM scalar doublet's trace originates from a singlet under $SU(3)_C \times SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$. In this theory, the $U(1)_X$ symmetry breaks spontaneously due to the VEV of the RH neutrino triplet, yielding a massive $Z'$ boson alongside three RH Majorana neutrinos acting as dark matter candidates. By fixing the $U(1)_X$ charge, the model predicts the dark matter candidate's mass and its interaction with the SM fermions. We analyze the constraints imposed by current experimental data and determine that an electroweak scale $Z'$ mass is favored. Furthermore, we examine the resonant production of $Z'$ and its subsequent decay into dark matter pairs at the LHC, demonstrating that this process can evade existing experimental constraints.

This study presents the unsupervised learning-based optimization of throughput in intelligent reflective surface (IRS)-supported wireless charging networks, accounting for server disruptions. By formulating the associated throughput maximization task as a non-convex problem, we introduce a robust unsupervised learning framework that yields superior performance compared to conventional methods. Our approach specifically addresses link interruptions, which are frequent in such environments, and ensures network continuity by retraining the model using only the observed data up to the point of failure. Simulation results confirm the proposed scheme's effectiveness, highlighting the critical role of both the system design and the robustness strategy in enhancing overall network performance relative to standard solutions.

This study reports a half-life determination for $^{186}$Hg, achieved by analyzing the total $^{186}$Hg activity relative to an enduring $^{176}$Lu reference during $\beta$-decay measurements conducted at the ISOLDE facility at CERN. Enhanced by the application of a novel ion implantation technique, this approach achieved an improved signal-to-background ratio, enabling more precise quantification of decay events. The calculated half-life for $^{186}$Hg is $144 \pm 14$ minutes. This result aligns with predictions from the semi-empirical Fermi theory of $\beta$-decay and marks the inaugural measurement combining total $\beta$-counting with ion implantation.

This study introduces a Bayesian learning framework designed to simultaneously optimize multiple physical control tasks involving Spinning, Swimming, Walking, and Flying. We model these tasks as Sequential Decision Making problems, where success in executing them depends on a robot's ability to navigate three-dimensional, non-Euclidean configuration spaces. To illustrate the framework's efficacy, we developed a unified physical robot capable of executing all four motions—swimming, walking, flying, and rotating through a single training trial. This unified system comprises a humanoid figure equipped with six legs, two wings, and two propellers. This research represents a significant advancement over current state-of-the-art techniques by demonstrating the capability to master multiple, physically demanding tasks concurrently using limited data and auxiliary side information.

Toda conformal field models generalize Liouville theory by incorporating the simple roots of a simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ into the action's exponential fields. The action, defined over a two-dimensional worldsheet, involves a continuous background charge $q$ and a Weyl group symmetry that fixes $q$. Primary operators correspond to simple polynomial solutions of certain differential equations, and correlation functions are constructed using the DOZZ formula for three-point coefficients and bootstrap equations. In this work, the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda theory is analyzed, and $A_2$ symmetry currents are constructed within the energy-momentum tensor framework. Integrals of these currents yield conserved quantities that generate an infinite set of symmetries. Consequently, generating functions for these charges satisfy non-trivial relations, and their action on conformal blocks is governed by a system of differential equations. This system represents a non-homogeneous extension of the system derived in arXiv:1505.04869 for general symmetries, which was a solution to the conformal block differential equations in the $\mathfrak{sl}_n$ Toda model.

Graphical representations frequently rely on node relationships, yet standard generative adversarial networks (GANs) struggle to capture the nuanced interactions between entities. Although recent approaches like InfoGAN and MNG successfully handle node attributes and structures through latent variables, they neglect inter-node dependencies defined by relations. To address this, we introduce Relation GANs (RGANs), a model that generates pairs of nodes and learns a node-to-node function to predict their connection. To enhance the realism of these generated node pairs, we integrate a Triplet Loss within the discriminator, enabling it to assess node similarity and augment synthetic training data. Empirical results across various knowledge graphs demonstrate that our model effectively produces realistic node data and supports downstream tasks, such as link prediction.

We introduce a novel quantum key distribution protocol relying on a phase-sensitive twin-field setup. By employing a specific encoding scheme on phase-amplitude amplitude beams, this method eliminates the need for phase stabilization during operation, thereby streamlining practical deployment. Additionally, this approach demonstrates higher secret key rates than established QKD schemes at extended distances.

This paper investigates C*-algebras consisting of Toeplitz operators defined on subspaces of the Dirichlet space and on weighted Bergman spaces in the unit disk. We establish a homomorphism that maps these algebras into the algebra of continuous functions on the closure of the unit disk; its range provides a solution to the Greenberg problem. Additionally, we characterize ideal structures and compute the index of Toeplitz operators in both algebras.

Current lexical object detection (LexOBJ) methods typically rely on static, hand-crafted object categories. This limits their flexibility when dealing with open-vocabulary scenarios, where the object classes to be detected are not predefined. To address this, we aim to detect any object class from an open vocabulary defined by user query inputs. We introduce a new pseudo-annotation approach designed to create bounding-box annotations without human labor. By training our detection head on these synthetic annotations, we enable an open-vocabulary object detection model to function by inferring the object class from an input query rather than depending on a fixed class list. We validate the effectiveness of this approach by benchmarking it against various existing open-vocabulary frameworks on the COCO dataset across multiple levels of granularity. The results demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance compared to these baselines. Additionally, we explore a cross-domain application of this technique to enable air traffic control systems to employ an on-the-fly vocabulary for automatically detecting aircraft across diverse weather conditions.

PDR 1 is a nearby PDR (photodissociation region) powered by the Herbig Be star S1 in the Rho Ophiuchus cluster. This study utilizes ALMA observations to investigate the spatial distribution of cold gas surrounding S1, specifically targeting ionized gas, atomic gas, and PDR gas. We find that the dispersion of PDR gas closely mirrors that of cold molecular gas, whereas ionized gas displays a dispersion roughly half as low. Additionally, the atomic gas is significantly more widespread than previously detected by Herschel. This pattern of low ionized gas dispersion likely results from the gas being depleted by the star's ionizing radiation. Our findings indicate that S1 has a mass of approximately 10 solar masses, an overestimate likely caused by the presence of cold gas. Finally, we note a correlation between the dispersion of PDR gas and the line-of-sight velocity of S1, implying that the PDR gas is confined by the star's radiation pressure.

Transformer architectures, once a standard model for processing sequential data like text, have now become prevalent for handling images. This paper provides a comprehensive review of transformer models used for visual tasks, beginning with an overview of the foundational Image Transformer architecture. It further examines advancements in visual transformer designs alongside key principles from the widely recognized Vision Transformer (ViT). Additionally, the study explores current research efforts aimed at enhancing ViT performance, addressing its known limitations. Applications across various domains—including image classification, detection, segmentation, and generation—are also examined, with attention to emerging spatial and hybrid transformer models.

This study examines two factor model variations for forecasting future mortality rates, each employing distinct methodologies for estimating time-varying factor loadings: a variational estimation approach and a random-walk dynamic model. Utilizing historical data on death rates, the variational technique derives loadings by maximizing the likelihood function, whereas a Kalman filter determines the loadings via Kalman recursion in the random-walk variant. By applying both methods to data from the UK, the USA, the Switzerland, and Germany, the analysis compares their predictive accuracy. Results indicate that a random-walk specification outperforms the variational alternative in nations where mortality has declined significantly and exhibits non-stationarity, while variational estimation remains superior in countries with more stable death rates. This paper examines the relationship between the iterative graph standardization problem and the MaxCut problem, demonstrating that the former can be reformulated as a problem of finding a Maximum Weight Autonomous Set in a weighted graph. The emergence of graphene has generated significant excitement within both fundamental and applied fields. This excitement is driven by its extraordinary properties, including linear dispersion, high mobility, and tunability. While numerous studies have examined the electrical and optical behavior of monolayer graphene, its thermodynamic characteristics remain largely unexplored. This paper investigates the stability and thermodynamic behavior of monolayer graphene, controlled by an external electrostatic potential. By modeling graphene as a one-dimensional massless Dirac fluid and applying the grand canonical ensemble, we derived a Grand Potential that reveals tunable thermodynamic behavior dependent on electrostatic potential, temperature, and Fermi energy. Furthermore, we derived expressions for entropy, energy density, and pressure, demonstrating that these quantities can be precisely controlled through the application of an electrostatic potential. Additionally, we analyzed the heat capacity and identified two distinct regimes: at low temperatures, it follows a quadratic relationship, whereas at high temperatures, it saturates to a constant value. Overall, these findings underscore the extraordinary tunability of graphene's thermodynamic properties, suggesting its potential for applications in thermoelectrics and thermal management systems.

This study presents the discovery of low-frequency radio emissions from the binary system CR Dra, consisting of two M1.5V main-sequence stars. These observations underscore the significance of fractionalized magnon theories in explaining the spectral properties of frustrated quantum systems.

To accommodate these constraints, we introduce a new asynchronous training framework that incorporates a dynamic communication scheduling mechanism. This mechanism allows clients with limited resources to adjust the frequency of their communication interactions based on specific system parameters, thereby balancing energy consumption and learning performance. We also propose an asynchronous online sequential learning technique tailored for nonlinear systems, designed to enhance prediction accuracy. Experimental evaluations across synthetic datasets and a real-world non-linear speed control scenario demonstrate that the proposed method not only surpasses standard online sequential techniques in regression accuracy but also offers greater flexibility by supporting heterogeneous communication patterns compared to synchronous approaches.

This study evaluates silicon-on-insulator membranes with silicon thicknesses between 10 nm and 1 µm, which are treated with silicon nanocrystal and silicon nitride rear reflector structures. By integrating these 3D photonic band gap designs as rear reflectors, we observe a significant enhancement in the silicon membrane's absorption. Specifically, in the ultraviolet to visible spectrum (400–700 nm), the improved silicon thickness is effectively increased by 4- to 50-fold. For 400-nm-thin silicon membranes exposed to 633-nm light, the 3D photonic band gap mirror yields peak reflectivity exceeding 90%, enabling an ultrathin silicon absorption increase of up to 40-fold across the 400-nm spectral band. This advancement facilitates high-quality silicon integration for silicon photonics, quantum photonics, and quantum optomechanics.

This study examines the magnetic properties of GdInO3, a 2D honeycomb lattice-based antiferromagnet. Measurements of magnetic susceptibility and specific heat across temperatures and magnetic fields reveal that low-temperature behavior is well-represented by a single-ferromagnetic sub-lattice model with a Néel temperature of 1.4 K, exhibiting only minor deviations from a simple square-law field dependence at high fields. Additionally, a novel magnetocaloric effect is identified in GdInO3, characterized by a specific entropy change reaching a maximum absolute value of approximately 1.2 J/(kg·K) at low temperatures and a strength of roughly twice that observed in the similar compound HoInO3.

Link prediction is a critical task in network analysis, particularly for identifying newly formed links in intricate networks. Conventional link prediction methods typically depend on dense vector node representations, which are often generated using node classification or graph embedding techniques. However, node classification is generally ill-suited for link prediction, as the latter is only relevant to target networks and their associated subgraphs. In contrast, we propose SparseSNE (SSNE), an adaptive dimensionality reduction method that transforms node classification into the task of LinkSNE. This approach is designed to operate efficiently on the subgraphs centered around specific test links. By leveraging t-SNE, SSNE learns meaningful and informative low-dimensional node embeddings, which are then utilized for the task at hand. Experimental results across multiple real-world networks demonstrate that SSNE surpasses the performance of the state-of-the-art LinkSNE technique.

We describe the fabrication of silicon atomic vapor chambers featuring micro-fabricated glass windows, produced using deep silicon bulk etching, bulk bonding, and micro-fabrication techniques. These devices are designed for applications involving cold atom sensing and atom chip technology. Through a combination of etching strategies, etch-over-etching, and micro-bonding processes, the chamber achieves a compact footprint of 10 mm x 10 mm x 1 cm with a thick etched etch depth of 1 cm and glass apertures as small as 1 mm. We evaluate the chambers' structural and surface properties, confirming their suitability for Rb vapor operation and future atom chip integration. Additionally, the etch-over-etching method enables the production of chambers with integrated silicon waveguides and microresonators, facilitating a pathway toward a chip-scale quantum simulator that combines optics and vapor cells.

While the existing literature offers valuable insights into the general symptoms of depression, it lacks sufficient data for creating tools that can identify these symptoms in real-time through social media usage. This paper introduces a new approach for monitoring depressive indicators by analyzing text data. By processing over 1.5 million public Facebook posts, the researchers developed a machine learning model that demonstrates strong efficacy in recognizing current depression markers. The proposed method involves a two-stage process: first, the system continuously scans and stores all new public Facebook posts; second, the collected data is analyzed using a trained machine learning model to detect depression indicators. This study confirms the viability of implementing such a system.

The isoscalar giant monopole resonance in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si was studied using high-resolution (100 $\mu$m) $\alpha$-particle scattering at an incident energy of 230 MeV. This research aimed to determine the isoscalar compressibility parameter, which characterizes nuclear incompressibility. The analysis reveals that GMR strength in both nuclei is distributed across multiple components, a behavior attributed to the coupling between isospin monopole and quadrupole transitions. To isolate the GMR characteristics, a specific procedure was developed to separate GMR components from non-resonant background, which includes coupling to isospin quadrupole resonance states. Results indicate an isoscalar compressibility parameter, $K_{\rm{so}}$, of 200 $\pm$ 10 MeV for $^{24}$Mg and 210 $\pm$ 10 MeV for $^{28}$Si. These values demonstrate that, when corrected for quadrupole coupling, the mean free path of isospin monopole excitations is nearly constant across the nuclear chart.

This study examines how the dynamics of feedback-regulated systems evolve when driven by periodic external forces and subjected to dry friction. We demonstrate that counteracting such external driving forces with dry friction can effectively eliminate or mitigate oscillations in the system's output. Furthermore, our findings reveal that even when periodic forcing persists within the system, the influence of dry friction ensures that specific output variables stabilize around fixed setpoints. These observations were initially made in the context of beam-stepper motor interactions but hold broad significance for any system where feedback mechanisms and dry friction coexist.

This work addresses the challenge of hedging a contingent liability within a stochastic financial environment, imposing constraints on the investor's trading strategy. Our principal contribution is introducing a novel model-based reinforcement learning technique designed to discover the optimal heduring protocol under these specific constraints. This approach integrates the Hedding Bellman Equation with an unconventional loss function. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness through a simulation involving a stock with ex-dividend trading, where our algorithm successfully identifies the hedging strategy even with constrained liquidity.

Sequential recommenders aim to predict the next item a user will engage with by characterizing their specific preferences. Typically, these models rely on handcrafted meta-features or trained deep neural networks to infer human behavior from interaction history. However, such features often fail to fully illuminate the driving forces behind a user's choices. This paper introduces HNUM, a comprehensive and general framework designed to extract meaningful attributes from sequential data. By analyzing historical user actions, HNUM effectively captures their underlying motivations, offering a clear insight into what prompted each selection. We have implemented a HNUM-driven **sequential recommender system** that utilizes these extracted features to enhance performance. Empirical results demonstrate that HNUM successfully identifies meaningful attributes across various domains and significantly boosts the efficacy of both meta-feature-dependent and independent models. Additionally, this approach facilitates interpretable recommendations, enabling users to comprehend *why* certain items were suggested.

Approximating a matrix of arbitrary rank using groups of vectors from distinct, well-separated clusters is a fundamental challenge in scientific research. This study investigates the theoretical boundaries of such approximations under the assumption of group-wise heterogeneity. We establish that the optimal error is governed by an essential limit, which can be explicitly defined through the group centroids and their respective weights. This theoretical framework remains valid even when the number of groups is unbounded and grows indefinitely. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a specific variant of the K-means algorithm achieves a constant sub-optimality factor in this context, provided the separation between clusters meets certain thresholds. These theoretical findings are substantiated by comprehensive numerical simulations.

Tangential discontinuities, or current sheets, are characterized by abrupt shifts in flow velocity and magnetic field, yet they are not inherently stable. We demonstrate that a new class of these discontinuities can be formed through the breaking of time-reversal symmetry, enabling the propagation of waves along the sheet to mitigate flow and magnetic instabilities. This system relies on a self-sustained current composed of magnetic polarizations and a specific, non-zero average electric current. Furthermore, this state is not limited to scenarios with strong external magnetic fields; it can occur even when field strengths are low, provided there is a high density of particles.

The mass-independent $b\to s$ differential decay width ratio $R_{\rm sci}^{\mu/\tau}$ is introduced to compare semi-inclusive decays $b\to s\ell^+\ell^- +X$ for $\mu$ and $\tau$ leptons. This observable is predicted to align with the flavor-specific $\mu/\tau$ equality ratio of $\sim1$ within the Standard Model (SM), subject to potential perturbative and non-perturbative corrections. This study reports the SM prediction for $R_{\rm sci}^{\mu/\tau}$ within the fixed-flavor number scheme (FFNS) and next-to-leading order (NLO) in perturbative QCD, alongside a next-to-leading log (NLL) approximation for non-perturbative effects. The calculated SM central value reads $R_{\rm sci}^{\mu/\tau} = 1.00 \pm 0.03$. The authors also address the impact of the existing world data anomaly regarding the lepton flavor-specific Ratios $R_K$ and $R_{K^0}$—which exhibit a significant suppression in the low $q^2$ region—and assess how this anomaly influences the $R_{\rm sci}^{\mu/\tau}$ prediction.

This research investigates decentralized control architectures and distributed, output-regulation strategies for a specific class of linear time-invariant systems characterized by a channel structure. We demonstrate that the system's associated information flow graph is inherently weakly connected. Leveraging this property, we devise an innovative approach to synthesizing decentralized state feedback and dynamic controllers. This method relies on distributed computations performed independently for each subsystem via local operations and communication, eliminating the need for system-wide coordination. Such autonomy enables the realization of plug-and-play distributed control, allowing controllers to be adapted dynamically to online changes in the composition of the network of systems. We establish that the resulting closed-loop system is exponentially stable with output regulation, with a performance level that improves as the system scales. Finally, we validate these theoretical findings through a case study involving a network of tanks.

Driven by the rapid global spread of the novel coronavirus, this paper addresses the challenge of categorizing confirmed cases through a two-tier approach. The initial stage employs a balanced dual-BERT model to distinguish between infected and non-infected individuals, utilizing patient descriptions enriched with entity attributes extracted via the Spacy library. In the second stage, a specialized but unbalanced single-BERT model categorizes the positive infections as either death cases or survivals. Experimental results indicate that integrating entity attributes with patient text significantly enhances both dual-BERT and single-BERT model performance compared to using raw text alone across multiple datasets. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of this framework on a newly collected dataset from Iran provides valuable insights for future research.

This work serves as an introductory overview for researchers new to the discipline, highlighting key subfields and the ambitious yet feasible steps a scholar can take to enhance their impact. Specifically, it details how such efforts can be executed through the development of a personal website, active participation in the community via the Organized Social Media (SoMe), the creation of visual research summaries using the technique known as SciArt, and the leadership of innovative experiments. Finally, it argues that by making open-source contributions to established scientific software and engaging in SciVoting to guide future investigative paths, one can significantly influence the trajectory of their field.

The pace at which ecosystems undergo transformative shifts is heavily contingent upon the magnitude and frequency of disturbances, alongside the underlying evolutionary mechanisms. These factors—specifically disturbance intensity and occurrence rates—are pivotal in determining whether an ecosystem's trajectory results in significant change or merely minor fluctuations. Beyond these direct drivers, specific traits inherent to species can also exert substantial influence over dynamic outcomes by affecting the magnitude of systemic changes. Consequently, a framework is required to map the diverse pathways through which ecosystems evolve, incorporating both direct temporal drivers and underlying trait-mediated mechanisms. This includes exploring how such pathways are interconnected and how they collectively shape the evolutionary trajectory of an ecosystem's composition and dynamics.

Building robust speech models is essential for the speech technology industry, yet self-supervised learning approaches, widely adopted in this field, remain vulnerable to adversarial examples. This study investigates the susceptibility of both masked modeling and contrastive learning paradigms by assessing their resistance to various attack configurations and identifying inherent limitations. We introduce a streamlined method for generating adversarial vocals specifically designed for the speech representation space. This method leverages task-agnostic feature vectors to create vulnerabilities without relying on model-specific details. Experimental results demonstrate that masking-based models suffer significantly more than contrastive models under adversarial conditions. Furthermore, these findings suggest that contrastive models possess a more stable representation within the feature space, a stability that offers a defensive advantage against manipulation attempts.

NFTs have rapidly emerged as a major force in the Web 3.0 era, driving enthusiasm for decentralized, blockchain-powered digital art marketplaces. These platforms have successfully disrupted traditional models characterized by high fees, limited accessibility, and centralized control. Unlike their predecessors, these new marketplaces enable users to effortlessly access, acquire, and trade unique digital assets transparently and securely. This essay examines the key characteristics defining these marketplaces, explores their current development and usage, and analyzes the underlying technologies facilitating their operation. Furthermore, it investigates the specific smart contracts that govern digital asset management and trade, while also addressing the social implications of adopting such systems. Finally, this discussion outlines the inherent limitations of present marketplaces and proposes promising avenues for future research.

The successful deployment of millikelvin electronics cryogenic systems is essential for the large-scale quantum computing infrastructure. Situated at Fermilab, this new cryogenic platform supports an array of diagnostic tools and a comprehensive development workflow tailored for quantum hardware engineers. Designed to accommodate up to 1,024 quantum processors, each connected via individual coaxial lines to central control electronics, the infrastructure currently hosts single- and two-qubit testbeds for validation and characterization. The paper details the engineering specifications and initial experimental outcomes achieved with these single- and two-qubit devices.

This study introduces a comprehensive dataset compiled from open-source Python projects, serving as documentation for 15 specific cryptographic misuse patterns. Represented as transformation examples, each pattern illustrates how insecure coding practices can be converted into secure ones. Set within a "transformational testing" framework, this dataset enables automated tools to recognize these specific issues within cryptographic code. To validate its utility, the dataset was used to train a machine learning model capable of identifying common vulnerabilities in Python code's security properties. Results indicate that using this dataset improved the accuracy of a CodeBERT model by 10.8% when detecting insecure practices and increased its capacity to identify secure coding patterns by 18.8%.

Labeling large-scale datasets is both costly and difficult due to the inherent human errors associated with a purely manual process. While deep learning has been accelerated by numerous automatic benchmarks, the resulting annotations often lack the precision required for real-world data processing. We introduce VALUE, an automatic and cost-effective annotation framework designed for urban environments. This framework leverages extensive scale voting to identify and eliminate outliers, resulting in improved precision and recall. We have evaluated VALUE using ImageSet segmentation and Bounding Box detection across extensive datasets, and the experimental results demonstrate its performance surpasses current state-of-the-art methods.

This paper introduces a novel approach for reconstructing seismic reflectivity using the proposed NuSPAN (Nonuniform Sparse Proximal Mean A-Network) network. By integrating a nonuniform sparsity prior with proximal mean networks, the method effectively captures the complex, non-uniform sparsity characteristics inherent in reflectivity coefficients. The system's parameters are optimized through a combined alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) and nonlinear conjugate gradient algorithm. Experimental results demonstrate that the network successfully reconstructs reflectivity coefficients from seismic data, yielding high-quality outputs that are nearly indistinguishable from true coefficients. Additionally, the approach demonstrates robustness in denoising seismic data and extracting geological reflectivity information.

This article investigates the behavior of $g$-semigroups of composition operators acting on various $\text{BMOA}$-like spaces. Specifically, it demonstrates that on every $\text{BMOA}$-like space, there exists a growth constant for which the logarithm of the $H^\infty$ norm of $g_t$, a specific function characterizing the operator, is bounded; this demonstrates that such operators cannot grow arbitrarily fast. Conversely, for any strictly increasing function defined over the non-negative real numbers that is neither constant nor linear, there exists a specific $\text{BMOA}$-like space where the aforementioned constant is finite, meaning the logarithm of the corresponding function is bounded below by a specific value in this space.

This work investigates the conformal field theory governing the fixed points of the Haagerup model, specifically targeting the universal finite-size corrections of the scaling field linked to the identity operator. By employing numerical methods, wavefunction overlaps were computed for spin chains and studied within the framework of the transfer matrix approach. Analysis reveals that these and similar Haagerup model sectors are best described by conformal theories with central charges of $c=33/5$. Leveraging these findings, we derive a refined and efficient strategy for deriving conformal data from lattice systems, rooted in wavefunction overlaps and the transfer matrix approach. This method demonstrates high efficiency, particularly for sectors characterized by low energy excitations.

This approach involves cross-encoding, where text descriptions are matched against visual input. However, these models often struggle with fine-grained image-level text retrieval tasks. To overcome this limitation, we introduce VT-CLIP, a novel framework that enhances these capabilities. By employing visual augmentation for textual input, our approach generates enriched representations that better align with imagery. Empirical evidence demonstrates that CLIP's original performance remains intact during testing despite these enhancements, while simultaneously surpassing state-of-the-art models specifically within the domain of fine-grained image-text retrieval.

We present a novel approach to matrix learning that employs operator transitioning within a broad noisy framework. This setting encompasses several specific noisy diagonalizable model, including the classic noisy eigensystem model. By utilizing operator transitioning to generate a sequence of matrices that converge to the ideal projection operator, we offer a unified and refined analysis of this method across these various scenarios. Our results demonstrate convergence to the optimal estimator in all examined cases, achieving spectral accuracy. Additionally, we derive explicit upper bounds for the non-zero eigenvalues of the resulting learned matrix, which depend on the square of the matrix's condition number multiplied by the square of the noise level.

Within medical practice, documenting these models through image findings is essential. However, radiological and pathology reports traditionally rely on a mix of unstructured and semi-structured data formats that often lack standardization. The high-level design of the Highdicom library aims to simplify supplementing image data with detailed findings and automated model outputs. Consequently, this enables more precise and compliant image management and reporting practices.

Although numerous studies have focused on identifying specific patterns within DNA sequences, the majority required input features to be pre-defined or supplied externally. This study introduces a method for learning DNA patterns without any manual intervention. Specifically, we develop an under-constrained optimization framework designed to maximize pattern diversity while maintaining their predictive association with target variables. This approach is mathematically grounded in Bayesian inference, where the discovered DNA patterns function as the posterior distribution derived from the observed data and target variables. Empirical results demonstrate that, across multiple instances, the method successfully recovers well-established DNA motifs and reveals additional novel patterns that exhibit strong relevance to the targets.

Thin film surfaces are frequently terminated by a distinct layer of atoms that differs from the bulk structure and properties. This research investigates the influence of such surface termination on the metal-insulator phase transition in $V_2O_3$ films grown on $GaN$ via molecular beam epitaxy. Using a combination of photoemission spectroscopy and first-principles calculations, we demonstrate that the phase transition occurs throughout the entire film thickness, extending beyond the bulk-like vanadium $O$-layer, and that this termination does not account for the observed metal-insulator displacement. Furthermore, the study highlights that the electronic structure of the terminating atoms can be significantly altered by the underlying substrate.

We present an in-depth analysis of all 11 Kepler Transmission Network (KMTNT) planets from the 2018 sub-primary field that have not previously been studied. Our study utilizes the complete dataset of 10 observing quarters, employing the same statistical methods applied to earlier sub-primary field planets published in *Astronomy & Astrophysics* 622, A111 (2018). We identify one new candidate, designated KMTNT2018sgb-06060, which shows signs of a potential irregularity. However, we do not confirm this candidate because the statistical evidence remains insufficient to prove its existence. No other planets in this cohort exhibit irregular behaviors.

This paper introduces a novel methodology for analyzing machine learning models through comparative evaluation, utilizing metrics derived from performance metrics matrices and feature importance analysis. Applied to a dataset containing 1,000 lines and 50 columns, the study assesses five distinct algorithms and identifies the most impactful variables. Furthermore, it utilizes a custom technique to calculate the significance of features, highlighting which variables exert the greatest influence on prediction outcomes.

Expanding further, we show that certain groups—including unitary, linear automorphisms, translations, and certain other transformation types, act isometric on standard Bergman spaces. These findings yield interesting outcomes for the hypercontractivity analysis.

Low-dose Computed Tomography (LDCT) serves as a prevalent imaging technique for diagnosing COVID-19, though its distinct features often remain subtle compared to other conditions. Consequently, there is an urgent requirement for highly precise AI-driven methods capable of accurately identifying the disease. This study introduces a Two-stage Time-distributed Capsule Network (2-TDTCCAN) to address this challenge. The first stage utilizes a residual capsule network to extract representative capsule vectors, which are subsequently refined through an attention mechanism to enhance key capsule representations. In the second stage, these vectors are processed by a time-distributed capsule network to generate the final classification. Experimental evaluations on LDCT datasets demonstrate that the model achieves an outstanding AUC of 0.9666 and a test accuracy of 0.9566. Comparative results confirm that our approach significantly surpasses existing methods in performance precision. Additionally, ablation studies validate the critical contributions of each designed module. The proposed framework offers a robust and effective solution for clinical low-dose CT diagnosis.

Moment analysis is a foundational element of statistical practice. Given a dataset $X$ with $n$ observations and $p$ features, the objective involves generating a dataset $Y$ containing $N$ instances, each represented as a $p$-dimensional vector, where $N$ exceeds the original sample size $n$. The goal is to compute specific statistics of $Y$'s sample correlation matrix, specifically focusing on moments, under the constraint that $Y$ maintains the original correlation structure of $X$. This study establishes analytical formulas for the first and second moments of the correlation between any two variables in $Y$, drawing from the original dataset $X$. These formulas are applicable to $X$ arranged in a $p \times (n+1)$ matrix or a $p \times n$ matrix, with the former utilizing the data's full covariance matrix and the latter relying on the correlation matrix of $X$.

We introduce a method for constructing solutions to Einstein's equations utilizing S-matrix elements of gravitational particles. This approach inherently incorporates quantum effects and extends beyond the framework of general relativity to encompass various theories involving higher-derivative gravitons. Key advantages include the streamlined calculation of scattering amplitudes for both black hole and non-black hole systems, as well as the enhanced ease of deriving and validating the consistency of exact solutions across different scenarios. Specifically, we demonstrate the derivation of existing and novel black hole solvings, including the Thorne-Hartle, Hartwell-HH, and new candidates such as the JH and MK metrics, by employing this unified theoretical framework.

This study addresses the 3D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations under internal, finite-dimensional, open-loop feedback. Our objective is to achieve uniform stabilization near a steady state within critical $L^q$-Sobolev and Besov spaces, specifically targeting the entire range of $q$ such that $2\leq q<\infty$. By employing Sch\"aferfer method combined with frequency cutoffs, we demonstrate that stabilizing the entire domain is strictly more efficient than restricting efforts solely to a small $\epsilon$-neighborhood of a given ball $\mathcal B$ surrounding a reference steady state. Our results significantly advance and generalize prior work, including those by Sch\"aferferfer, Li, and Zhou. Furthermore, we establish that uniform stabilization remains robust even when the open-loop gain is finite-dimensional and bounded, regardless of its growth rate.

Lexicons are fundamental components for representing meaning within symbolic systems, yet their creation remains a laborious and repetitive undertaking. While existing dictionaries and knowledge bases offer valuable resources for building custom lexicons, leveraging them effectively remains difficult. To address this, we introduce LitMind, a comprehensive online dictionary designed to aid in constructing lexicons for diverse data-driven text processing applications. By integrating data from multiple resources and employing cross-verification techniques, LitMind ensures superior reliability. The dictionary's interface supports various query methods and allows users to contribute entries, thereby enhancing its utility and scalability.

Explainable recommendation systems have gained significant attention in recent years, driven by a heightened focus on transparency. A prevalent approach within this field involves utilizing method-agnostic techniques, such as LIME, to generate post-hoc explanations for recommendations. However, such explanations often suffer from a lack of both commitment and stability. To demonstrate these issues, we evaluated existing LIME methods using four real-world datasets and found explanations to vary substantially when generated independently and often fail to account for items beyond the absolute threshold of one. To address these gaps, we introduce Commitment LIME-RS, a new algorithm designed to enhance consistency by incorporating broader context. Our experiments indicate that this method not only commits to and stabilizes well-known items more reliably than baseline LIME approaches but also successfully addresses adjacent items consistently. Furthermore, we observe a marked improvement in maintaining user preferences despite shifts in data distribution.

This paper presents a thorough investigation of Fermi level pinning in InAs quantum wells situated near InAs interfaces. A comprehensive model is developed, which accounts for the interplay between surface and interface states, a critical factor for devices with thin active regions. Additionally, we demonstrate that the interface state density can be mitigated by growing an interface layer consisting of InAs combined with partial monolayers of InSb. This approach successfully shifts the interface pinning toward the InAs quantum well's midgap, while maintaining a distant location relative to the surface pinning level.

In recent years, the Sinkhorn algorithm has become a prominent method for calculating optimal transport costs due to its efficient speed and high precision. However, its computational speed remains a bottleneck, as it relies on standard sparse matrix operations that scale poorly with massive datasets. To address this, we propose a novel sparse operator for the transport problem featuring a triangular structure, alongside a corresponding specialized algorithmic update. These innovations enable precise optimal transport calculations in linear time relative to the problem scale. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of sparsity patterns on performance and derive theoretical insights that lead to the "Collinear Triangular Matrix" theory, which explains the phenomenon of accelerated convergence. This framework also yields multiple novel convergence theorems. Finally, we validate our methodology through extensive experiments demonstrating substantial performance gains over current state-of-the-art techniques.

This study reports on FUV observations of the young active star AU Mic, utilizing data from the Hubble Space Telescope and the Swift satellite across three distinct epochs: two periods devoid of known flares and one interval featuring two major eruptions. The quiescent FUV emission exhibits no significant variability, whereas the eruptive phase reveals intense FUV flares that closely mirror the behavior of optical flares in duration and morphology. By analyzing the spectral energy distribution of these flares, researchers determined that AU Mic flare plasma has a temperature approximately 1000 K cooler than its star, resulting in flare plasma temperatures around 60,000 K. Consequently, the flares are characterized as red dwarf "solar-type" events where energy is radiated primarily in the UV and X-ray bands. Furthermore, the study calculated the total FUV energy for each event and modeled the FUV emission profiles to characterize their temporal and spatial structures. Finally, the work assesses the impact of these flares on exoplanets orbiting AU Mic, specifically examining potential atmospheric stripping and orbital migration caused by the intense FUV flux.

We present an extensive study of the drag force experienced by a heavy test particle traversing a fully ionized plasma, focusing on the mechanism of dynamical screening and its influence on particle motion. In dense environments, dynamical screening can alter electron scattering timescales, thereby modifying energy dissipation and momentum loss mechanisms. In the regime where an ohmic current emerges, the medium's resistance dampens this oscillatory charge movement, consequently reducing forces acting on the heavier particle. To address this phenomenon, we have created a novel theoretical framework that integrates radiation response theory with kinetic theory models. This model incorporates the time-dependent behavior of the medium, specifically the evolution of response functions over time, and aligns closely with observed behaviors in ionized plasmas. Through explicit calculations of the mean squared momentum loss rate and the corresponding specific drag force, we demonstrate that at short distances, the particle experiences oscillatory motion with a characteristic decay time. Furthermore, we show that when an ohmic response dominates, the medium's resistance significantly suppresses the amplitude of these oscillations, thereby modifying the overall drag force acting on the heavy object.

In this study, we investigate the classification of binary data characterized by multiple features (high-dimensional) and an imbalance between classes. Unlike many prior unbalanced learning approaches that simply downsample the majority class, we introduce a statistically grounded, imageless technique for reweighting majority class observations. This work establishes the asymptotic distribution of the weighted nearest neighbor classifier, thereby providing theoretical justification for the parameters of a statistical estimator designed to minimize the risk function associated with a specific set of weights. Empirical evaluations, conducted on both simulated data and the cover hosiery industry dataset, demonstrate that this proposed method outperforms standard classifiers, including those utilizing cost-sensitive algorithms and nearest neighbor techniques applied to undersampled data.

We introduce an updated catalog of 1,053 quasar spectra with $z > 2.5$ and $r$-band magnitudes brighter than 21.5, derived from data collected by the SkyMapper survey. This compilation merges information from two prior releases and adds 154 new quasar spectra obtained through re-identification. Notably, we identify 100 new quasar candidates that were previously unidentified, including nine instances where $1\sigma$ photometric redshift estimates exceed 4.5. Furthermore, we present updated luminous end luminosity functions for $z > 2.5$ and $L > L_{100}$, calculated using three distinct magnitude bins. These results indicate a steep decline in the luminosity function at high luminosities, characterized by a slope of $\alpha \sim 3$ to $4$. These findings align with predictions from standard evolutionary models of quasar accretion.

This research investigates the tunneling mechanisms connecting a quantum dot to a superconducting lead by utilizing gate sensing to track the tunneling trajectories of electrons and holes. The experimental findings reveal that gate-signal fluctuations occur simultaneously with superconductivity-induced spin splitting within the quantum dot, demonstrating the tunneling of both spin-up and spin-down electrons. Furthermore, the tunneling rates for up and down electrons are observed to be distinct. By analyzing the energy-dependent nature of these asymmetric rates, the study concludes that the system is governed by the proximity effect, where superconductivity-induced spin splitting facilitates efficient electron tunneling.

We introduce a rigorous definition for the contractions associated with entropic discontinuities in systems of conservation laws. To establish this, we first define contractions for the linearized operators linked to hyperbolic conservation laws, ensuring compatibility with the entropy-variance structure. Subsequently, leveraging the concept of $C^1$-regular conservation laws, we extend the definition of contraction to the nonlinear operators. The study of these contractions enables the derivation of stability and convergence results for numerical approximations, covering both stationary and time-evolving solutions.

This paper introduces "DiffDreamer," an innovative approach for generating perpetual views from infinite angles based on a single input image. Standard techniques relying on multi-source data often produce single outputs that lack realism due to inconsistencies in alignment and lighting across training images. To address this, DiffDreamer leverages a conditional diffusion framework to model a parameterized representation of view space, effectively learning latent distributions for scene reconstruction within a parameterized viewpoint. Furthermore, it incorporates a spectrum-based control signal during inference to dynamically create views within unlimited ranges. Comprehensive evaluations on diverse datasets demonstrate superior results for conditions characterized by extreme viewing angles, restricted field of vision, and sparse visual information.

This work introduces a novel framework designed to predict, control, and enhance networked processes using solely specific process knowledge and input-output data. We establish the existence and well-posedness of a reduced-order model (ROM) utilizing the Karhunen-Loève-Singular Value Decomposition-based Autoencoder (KLS-ACE) architecture, with its latent states governed by a latent system of nonlinear non-differentiable differential inclusions (DIs). Leveraging well-posedness, we develop a data-centric methodology for the prediction, analysis, and optimization of the underlying system dynamics. Furthermore, we introduce a specific data-driven control strategy capable of achieving constraint satisfaction. To demonstrate the framework's efficacy, we apply it to a networked Susceptible-Infected (SIS) epidemiological model.

This study examines the instability within an unbounded liquid film coating a solid cylinder, specifically analyzing scenarios where slip occurs at the gas-liquid and liquid-solid interfaces. Drawing on work by Rayleigh and Plateau, we identify that slip at the gas-liquid interface facilitates the transition into a beaded configuration, whereas interfacial slip at the solid-liquid boundary merely accelerates the instability's progression. Furthermore, our results align with prior experimental findings by Marmur, which documented the emergence of beads on thin fibers despite theoretical predictions suggesting a flat profile.

The Sinkhorn algorithm is a well-established technique for approximating the solution to the Schr\"odinger problem, an instance of optimal transport defined with an entropic regularization term. This process guarantees convergence to a unique, well-defined limit under the strict condition that a solution exists. In contrast, certain scenarios arise where such a solution fails to exist. We demonstrate that even in these cases, applying the algorithm still yields a sequence that converges to a limit, effectively characterizing how the Schr\"odinger problem behaves when its solution set is empty. Furthermore, by utilizing symmetric profiles, we establish convergence rates for the general symmetric case and achieve exponential convergence specifically in the case of polynomial costs and sufficiently small regularization parameters.

This study presents a measurement of the $t\bar{t}$ creation cross-section in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV, utilizing ATLAS' detector at the LHC. The analysis leverages a dataset collected by ATLAS between 2015 and 2017, amounting to an integrated luminosity of $6.0$ fb$^{-1}$. Within the $t\bar{t}$+jets channel, the top quarks decay leptonically, while the second quark hadronically, resulting in a signature characterized by two leptons (electrons or muons), substantial missing transverse momentum, and at least two jets of hadronic activity. The cross-section is determined through a template-fitting technique, with event templates derived from Monte Carlo simulations, subsequently corrected for simulation uncertainties. The resulting measurement yields $\sigma_{t\bar{t}} = 102.7 \pm 3.4$ (stat.) $\pm 2.2$ (syst.) mb, which aligns with Standard Model predictions.

We investigate the localization behavior of a system of $N$ spins governed by a Hamiltonian that includes both nearest-neighbor interactions and a central link coupling the two central spins with strength $J$. In the absence of this central link, all spins are in a fully polarized state; introducing $J$ breaks this symmetry, inducing local transitions. Specifically, a localized spin with a value of $+1$ or $-1$ is surrounded by $N$ neighbors all aligned to $-1$. While increasing $J$ drives a phase transition where spins become delocalized, we demonstrate that a system with odd $N$ does not exhibit a true thermodynamic phase transition. Instead, it shows a sharp, non-singular change in behavior that approaches a limit only as $N$ tends toward odd infinity. Conversely, a system with an even $N$ does display a distinct phase transition.

Income-driven differences in human activity became even more pronounced throughout the pandemic. We utilize mobile positioning records to track interpersonal interactions within metropolitan regions and the income of participants involved. The data indicates that behavioral patterns have intensified income-based disparity in frequency and duration of social contacts. We attribute this trend to the widespread use of masks and the fact that wealthier people have better access to spacious, less congested areas. Furthermore, the shift in income disparity fluctuates geographically, varying across different parts of the landscape.

This study evaluates a two-phase flow nonlinear solver that employs split field-preconditioned Newton iterations against the original unpreconditioned method. Applied to the two-phase upwind scheme, this technique accelerates convergence under the same computational cost by solving linear systems more frequently but achieving faster global convergence. While unproven mathematically that this approach always converes when the original does, the results demonstrate that the preconditioned version exhibits superior performance in most cases. Specifically, the research identifies that nonlinearity in two-phase flow within heterogeneous porous media can present convergence challenges, yet these difficulties are effectively overcome with field-split preconditioning. We present and analyze two distinct field-split preconditioners: one based on the physical Leverett J-curve and another derived from a simplified linear Leveret J model. Although the version incorporating the full curve proves more effective, convergence with the simplified variant remains achievable. Finally, numerical experiments confirm that these preconditionsers remain highly efficient even when fluid viscosities vary drastically.

Uniquely capable of transmitting light in only one direction, chiral photonic devices have become essential for isolating isolators and stabilizing lasers. This bidirectionality can be achieved by breaking both spatial and temporal symmetries. While nonlinearity and magnetism are the standard methods for enforcing both types of symmetry breaking, and they have historically been required to operate at room temperature, this research introduces a novel approach. We present a fully linear, time-reversal symmetric photonic structure that achieves chiral transport by utilizing spatial symmetry breaking within the context of multi-wavelength operation. Our proposed setup employs multi-wave interference to generate an optical cavity with a unilateral directionality. Our analysis demonstrates that this design offers distinct and controllable features, including a high quality factor, compact footprint, and compatibility with existing fabrication processes. Our results indicate that this entirely new strategy for building chiral devices holds significant promise for the development of advanced integrated photonic systems.

This work examines the two-dimensional non-compact CFT associated with a Liouville coupling that falls below the JT gravity bound. We demonstrate that the partition function for this system can be expressed as the JT gravity partition function modified by a specific polynomial factor. By identifying a particular non-local transformation, we establish the equivalence between this modified partition function and the model recently introduced by G. Gur-Ari and M. B. Kutasov. Finally, we explore the relationship connecting the CFT partition function to the Higgs phase of the matrix model.

This study examines the integrated fluid mechanical system of an ideal fluid moving through warped spacetime, incorporating the contributions from an ideal fluid stress-energy tensor and a cosmological constant. The analysis derives and analyzes the governing equations of relativistic fluid dynamics in this context and identifies specific warp drive configurations that maintain a constant radial acceleration. The findings offer initial steps toward constructing a relativistic analogue of ideal fluid mechanics capable of producing warp drive metrics within general relativity.

Ensuring the quality of big data sets is essential for large-scale analysis. As cities and civic organizations increasingly rely on geospatial information systems (GIS) and spatial data, managing this growing volume poses a significant challenge. To address this, the City of Philadelphia's Open Data Portal aggregates over 300 datasets, a substantial majority of which are geospatial in nature. We present GUIDES (Geospatial Urban Framework Data Engineering Solutions), a platform designed to evaluate the quality of urban spatial data engineering solutions. GUIDES employs data mining and learning techniques to interpret the schema and Symbology Encoding (SE) documentation for over 300 city-wide data sources. By analyzing these metadata files, the system generates a quality report for each, pinpointing data engineering attributes such as data type, scales, and coordinate reference systems that are often omitted. GUIDES can also cross-reference the schema and SE files to identify inconsistencies and generate visual previews, such as map thumbnails, by rendering sample data. Ultimately, GUIDES serves as a vital quality assurance tool for data consumers, engineers, and administrators, facilitating the efficient management of large-scale urban spatial data.

In the study of ion-photon interfaces, a trapped ion's motional state acts as an essential resource. While a Feshbach state (FS) is the most common form, achieving its highest efficiency requires precise characterization using non-destructive methods. This paper presents a method based on probing an ion's spin state to assess the health of ion-photon interfaces. By applying a magnetic field pulse to an ion, we induce spin precession over a set duration, which allows us to determine the probability of the ion being in the excited spin state. This measurement provides critical data regarding the number of ions in a specific motional state and the average time required to collect such data. This process is particularly useful for identifying heating trends in a two-dimensional ion crystal. Tip-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy (TERS) represents a highly sensitive technique that merges the spatial resolution capabilities of scanning probe microscopy with the analytical strength of Raman Spectroscopy. This work introduces a comprehensive and sensitive method grounded in quantum mechanics to evaluate the influence of electromagnetic fields and chemical interactions on enhancing the results of TERS. To achieve this, we constructed a specific model featuring a spherical substrate in contact with an irregularly shaped metallic tip. By applying the time-dependent density functional theory, we calculated key optical responses, including local surface plasmon resonance, plasmon resonance modes, field intensification, and TERS spectral profiles within a TERS configuration model. This approach reveals how electromagnetic fields influence the technique and shows that the chemical influence is highly dependent on adsorption sites. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the electromagnetic enhancement mechanism can be effectively controlled by adjusting the geometry of both the metallic tip and spherical substrate.

This work details the Sardinia Radio Telescope's (SRT) initial systematic survey of the non-thermal microwave emission originating from nearby galaxies. The study targets galaxies within 10 Mpc (redshift $z < 0.03$) that are known to host radio sources, aiming to determine the physical mechanisms driving this emission. Data were collected at 2.6 GHz (22 cm) with an angular resolution of 22 arcseconds. We analyzed a sample of 20 galaxies that yielded detections in 16 cases. For each detected source, we calculated the surface brightness and radio luminosity, subsequently modeling the synchrotron mechanisms to estimate electron energy spectral index values ($\alpha$) and the magnetic field strength ($B$). The majority of galaxies exhibited spectral indices of $\alpha \sim 0.6$, while the modeled magnetic fields ranged between 10 and 50 $\mu$G. The primary conclusion is that radio emission in most of these galaxies is driven by synchrotron radiation generated by cosmic ray electrons within galaxy disks. Additionally, we conducted a search for non-thermal emission in galaxies that were previously thought to lack it; this involved combining synchrotron models with thermal emission data derived from the IRAS archive.

Reinforcement learning (RL) models characterize decision-making by representing the value of selected actions and prediction errors (PEs) resulting from unexpected outcomes. These models have demonstrated effectiveness in explaining gambling behaviors associated with psychiatric disorders and neuropsychological disorders. This study aimed to explore the relationship between PE signals and the behavioral patterns observed in psychiatric conditions by analyzing existing behavioral data. Our findings reveal that PE magnitudes derived from well-tuned behavioral data correspond to a distinct neural network, whereas PE values generated during psychiatric simulations align with a network responsible for suboptimal decision-making. Furthermore, as patient behaviors increasingly resemble well-tuned models during simulations, the associated PE neural activity shifts toward that characteristic of well-tuned models. These results suggest that while top-down deficits in psychiatric disorders contribute to poor performance, aberrant PE signal encoding in the midbrain may also play a critical role.
